faqs.a: Thresholding compares every pixel's brightness to a cutoff value. Pixels brighter than the cutoff become white; darker ones become black. The result is a pure two-color image.
Each pixel is converted to luminance with the standard weights: 0.299 × red + 0.587 × green + 0.114 × blue. Green counts most because human eyes are most sensitive to green light.
Lower thresholds keep more pixels black (darker result); higher thresholds keep more white. For documents, start near 128 and adjust until the text is solid black on clean white.
faqs.q: Which threshold value should I use?

faqs.a: Thresholding destroys gradients and subtle shading — everything becomes pure black or white. For smooth black-and-white photos, a grayscale filter preserves tones better.

faqs.a: Inversion swaps black and white, useful for negative effects or for dark-mode versions of line art. It does not change which pixels pass the threshold, only their final color.

keyFacts: Thresholding reduces an image to exactly two colors: black and white.
Every pixel is first converted to a single brightness value (luminance).
Pixels at or above the threshold become white; the rest become black.
The standard luminance weights are 0.299 red, 0.587 green, 0.114 blue.
The effect is popular for stencil art, logos, QR-style graphics and OCR prep.
Large images are scaled to 1600 px on the long edge for fast processing.

image-threshold-filter.tagline: Pure black, pure white, no gray.
image-threshold-filter.workedExample:
Take one pixel with RGB (200, 150, 100) and threshold = 128.

Luminance = 0.299 × 200 + 0.587 × 150 + 0.114 × 100
         = 59.8 + 88.05 + 11.4
         = 159.25

159.25 ≥ 128, so the pixel becomes white (255, 255, 255).

With invert on, it would instead become black (0, 0, 0). Every pixel in the image is decided the same way, independently.
